prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Red, The

outputs.L1:
You find yourself in a narrow bed you’ve never slept in,  
on a tree-lined grassy field you’ve never walked upon,  
on a cold toilet seat you have not sat on,  
in a place you now call your home, your learning, your future.  

Red stone pathways reveal the buildings that will house  
the knowledge you seek  
and the information you wish to gather.  

You crane your neck to look up  
at the 13-story brick tower rising from the ground,  
looming over you as you walk past.  

The melodies and beats of different songs mingle,  
creating a sound of their own,  
flowing from open windows.  

Crushed leeks Top Ramen noodles, ground into a blue  
and speckled carpet, attract armies of ants  
to the communal kitchen on the sixth floor.  

You pull your jacket tighter against your body;  
a strong, salty wind whips off the Sound  
and up the hill as you walk through  
Red Square toward the clatter of knives,  
forks, and digesting bellies.  

Finally, you are released like a white dove  
from the hands of its owner, allowed to fly,  
discovering your dreams,  
discovering what you are made of.
outputs.L2:
You wake in a slim bed that has never held you before,  
in a grassy field edged with trees where your feet have never been,  
on a chilled toilet seat unfamiliar to your body,  
inside a place you now name as home, education, and tomorrow.  

Paths of red stone lead between the structures that will contain  
the understanding you are searching for  
and the facts you hope to collect.  

You tilt your head back to take in  
the thirteen-floor brick tower thrusting upward from the earth,  
casting its presence above you while you pass beneath it.  

From open windows, fragments of music drift out—  
rhythms and tunes from different songs blending together  
until they become a new noise of their own.  

Crumbled Top Ramen noodles with bits of leek,  
pressed into a blue, flecked carpet,  
draw lines of ants  
toward the shared kitchen on the sixth floor.  

You clutch your jacket closer,  
as a sharp, salt-heavy wind blows in from the Sound  
and climbs the hill with you  
while you cross Red Square  
toward the racket of cutlery  
and stomachs at work.  

At last, you are set free,  
like a white dove leaving its keeper’s hands,  
permitted to rise into the air—  
to uncover your ambitions,  
and to learn the substance of yourself.
outputs.L3:
The speaker arrives in an unfamiliar place, unsure of what to expect, but it quickly begins to take on a deeper meaning. What first seems strange and unknown soon becomes connected with the ideas of home, learning, and the future. The campus is not just a setting; it becomes a symbol of possibility. It is a place where the speaker can grow, study, meet new people, and begin imagining the life they want to build.

The physical details of the campus make this new world feel vivid and real. Red stone pathways stretch across the grounds, guiding students from one building to another. Tall brick buildings rise around the speaker, giving the campus a sense of history, strength, and importance. Above everything stands a 13-story tower, an impressive landmark that seems to watch over the entire place. These details help create an image of a campus that is both beautiful and intimidating, full of tradition but also full of opportunity.

Everyday dorm life is presented through small, sensory details that make the experience feel authentic. Music drifts out of open windows, suggesting the presence of other students and the energy of shared living. Inside the dorms, the carpets are messy, showing the chaos and reality of student life rather than an idealized version of it. In the communal kitchen, ants appear, adding humor and discomfort to the scene. These ordinary details show that campus life is not perfect, but it is lively, memorable, and deeply human.

The environment itself feels alive and demanding. Cold wind cuts across the campus, making the speaker aware of the physical challenges of this new place. The pathways are busy with students moving between classes, conversations, and responsibilities. Sounds fill the air, from voices and footsteps to music and the general noise of campus life. This atmosphere creates a sense of movement and pressure, as if the speaker has entered a world that is constantly active and expects them to keep up.

Ultimately, the experience represents much more than simply arriving at a school. It becomes a moment of freedom and self-discovery. The speaker is beginning to live independently, to make choices, and to understand who they are outside of the life they knew before. The campus becomes the starting point for pursuing dreams, facing challenges, and imagining a future shaped by their own ambitions. What began as an unfamiliar place becomes the beginning of a new chapter, filled with growth, possibility, and hope.
outputs.L4:
You arrive before you know how to arrive.

The car door opens, and the first thing you notice is the air. It is not the air from home. It smells faintly of cut grass, wet pavement, laundry detergent, and something metallic from the old radiators in the residence hall. Around you, cars idle with their trunks open like mouths. Parents carry boxes. Students drag suitcases over the sidewalk, the wheels clicking against every crack. Someone laughs too loudly. Someone is crying into a sweatshirt. Somewhere, a door keeps slamming.

You stand there for a moment with your backpack on one shoulder and your room key in your hand, feeling as if you have stepped into a place that has been waiting for you without knowing your name.

The campus map is folded wrong. The buildings look different in person than they did online. Their names blur together: Hall, Center, Library, Commons, North, West, Old, New. You follow signs and clusters of other students, pretending you understand where you are going. The sidewalk curves unexpectedly. A bell rings from a tower you had not noticed. Bicycles flash past. The trees are taller than you imagined, and the sky seems wider here, as if home had a lower ceiling.

Your residence hall smells like cardboard, floor cleaner, and nervous energy. The elevator is too small for all the people trying to use it, so you take the stairs, bumping your laundry basket against the wall. On the third floor, the hallway stretches ahead in a long strip of fluorescent light. Doors are propped open. Names are written on dry-erase boards. Music leaks from one room, then disappears behind another closing door. You hear the rip of packing tape, the scrape of furniture, the soft instructions of parents trying not to sound worried.

Your room is smaller than expected.

Two beds. Two desks. Two dressers. A window with a view of brick, branches, and a corner of the path below. The mattress is bare and blue, the walls blank, the floor dusty in the corners. For a second, disappointment rises in you, sharp and embarrassing. This is supposed to be your new home, but it looks like a room waiting to become one.

So you begin.

You unfold sheets. You stack books. You plug in a lamp. You tape photographs to the wall and arrange them carefully, as if the faces from home can keep the room from feeling strange. Your roommate asks where you are from. You ask the same question back. Both of you smile too much. You learn the first small facts: who brought a fan, who forgot hangers, who likes sleeping by the window, who is pretending not to be scared.

By evening, your parents are gone.

Their car pulls away slowly, and you wave until it turns the corner. Then your hand drops. The silence that follows is not really silence; campus is full of noise. Students shout across the quad. A skateboard rattles over the bricks. Doors open and close. Somewhere, a group is singing, badly but with confidence. Still, something inside you goes quiet. The space where your old life used to press close around you has opened, and for the first time you can feel its absence.

You return to your room and do not know what to do with yourself.

At home, the evening had a shape. Dinner, dishes, familiar voices, the hallway light, the sound of someone else moving through the house. Here, nothing tells you what comes next. You can eat when you want. You can leave the room or stay. You can introduce yourself to the people down the hall, or you can sit on your bed and scroll through your phone, reading messages from friends who are also trying to sound excited.

This freedom is not immediately joyful. At first, it feels like being set down in the middle of a vast, bright room with no instructions.

The first days pass in fragments. You learn the route to the dining hall, then forget it and learn it again. You discover which staircase comes out near the mailroom and which one leads to a door that locks from the outside. You sit through orientation sessions in crowded auditoriums, listening to advice you will only understand later. You collect flyers for clubs you may never join. You eat meals with people whose names you repeat silently so you will not lose them. You smile, answer questions, ask where everyone is from, and begin to realize that everyone is asking because everyone needs something to hold onto.

The campus becomes a series of sensations before it becomes a place.

Morning is the hiss of showers through cinderblock walls, the slap of sandals in the hall, the smell of coffee drifting from paper cups. Afternoon is sunlight on library windows, the dry whisper of notebook pages, the hum of vending machines, the sudden panic of not knowing which classroom is yours. Night is laughter outside your window, cold pizza, desk lamps, the blue glow of laptops, the distant pulse of music from a party you may or may not attend.

You are always slightly lost.

You walk into the wrong building and pretend you meant to. You arrive early because you are afraid of being late. You sit in lecture halls among hundreds of strangers and feel both invisible and exposed. Professors speak quickly, assigning chapters, essays, problems, possibilities. Their words fill the room: research, argument, experiment, history, identity, responsibility. You write them down even when you do not yet know what they mean for you.

Slowly, the unfamiliar begins to loosen.

The path to class becomes automatic. The dining hall no longer feels like a test. You learn where the forks are, which line moves fastest, which table gets afternoon sun. You recognize faces. Someone waves. Someone remembers your name. The student at the front desk no longer has to remind you to tap your ID. The campus that once seemed like a maze starts to gather around you in patterns.

And you begin to change in ways too small to announce.

You do your own laundry and shrink a shirt. You schedule your own appointments. You stay up too late and regret it in the morning. You make choices no one at home sees: what to study, where to go, who to trust, when to speak, when to leave. Some choices are ordinary. Some feel enormous. All of them belong to you.

There are still moments when homesickness arrives without warning. It comes while brushing your teeth in a communal bathroom, or hearing a song from high school, or seeing a family unload groceries from a car. It comes when you are tired, when the room feels too quiet, when you realize no one here knows the full story of who you were before you arrived.

But there is also relief in that.

No one here knows every version of you. No one has already decided what you are like. You are not fixed in place by old expectations, old mistakes, old habits of being. Each morning, you wake in a narrow bed under a new ceiling and feel, even through uncertainty, the strange mercy of beginning again.

College does not become home all at once. It becomes home through repetition: the same walk under changing leaves, the same chair in the library, the same laugh from a friend across the hall, the same late-night conversation that starts with homework and ends with the future. It becomes home when you stop checking the map. It becomes home when you begin giving directions to someone else.

And somewhere in the middle of all this—between the first awkward introductions and the first real friendship, between getting lost and finding your way, between missing home and building another—you understand what has happened.

You have not simply moved into a room.

You have crossed into a life that is yours to make.

The disorientation has not disappeared, but it has changed shape. What once felt like fear now feels like possibility. The unknown is still there, stretching ahead in the form of classes, people, questions, failures, and futures you cannot yet imagine. But it no longer seems only threatening. It begins to feel open.

You arrived uncertain, carrying boxes and doubts, surrounded by strange buildings and unfamiliar voices. You arrived looking for the place where you belonged.

Now, step by step, sound by sound, choice by choice, you are learning that belonging is not something you find fully formed.

It is something you build.

And in building it, you begin to discover yourself.
outputs.L5:
You stand beneath the red sky, watching the last light fade behind the hills. The world feels quiet, as if it is holding its breath. In that moment, the ordinary becomes something more—the path ahead, the wind against your face, the distant sound of leaves moving in the dark.

Red is everywhere: in the clouds, in the flowers by the road, in the memory of a sunset you once thought you had forgotten. It is the color of courage, of warning, of love, of endings and beginnings. It reminds you that life is never only one thing.

The night comes slowly, but you do not turn away. You keep walking, carrying the warmth of that red light with you, knowing that even when the sky grows dark, something bright remains inside.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a second-person free verse poem about arriving as a freshman at the University of Washington, including dorm life, Red Square, a brick tower, wind off the Sound, and the feeling of independence.
counterfactuals.output:
You arrive with two suitcases  
and a key that feels heavier  
than it should.

Your dorm room waits—  
cinderblock walls, twin bed,  
a window fogged with September,  
someone’s music leaking through the door,  
the hallway already teaching you  
how many strangers  
can become a kind of weather.

You learn the elevator’s moods,  
the laundry room’s midnight hum,  
the soft bravery of eating alone  
until alone becomes simply  
a place to begin.

In Red Square, rain darkens the bricks  
beneath your shoes.  
Backpacks stream past like currents,  
voices crossing in every direction,  
and you stand there  
small and newly unsupervised,  
under the wide gray sky  
of a campus that does not yet know your name.

The brick tower rises nearby,  
steady as an old promise,  
its face turned toward bells, books,  
the long green shoulders of trees.  
You look up  
and feel time looking back—  
all those students before you  
arriving, doubting, becoming.

Then comes the wind off the Sound,  
cold enough to wake your lungs,  
salt-threaded, pushing through your jacket  
as if to say: go on.

So you do.

You cross the square.  
You climb the hill.  
You carry your coffee, your map,  
your untested courage.

And in the space  
between one building and the next,  
between who you were at home  
and who you are not yet,  
you feel it—  
the sudden, frightening gift  
of your own life  
opening in your hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid sensory poem describing the first days of college in Seattle, with imagery of a dorm room, communal kitchen, music from open windows, ants, Top Ramen, and walking to the dining hall.
counterfactuals.output:
**First Days, Seattle**

The dorm room sweats with unpacked cardboard,  
new sheets stiff as envelopes,  
a borrowed lamp throwing honey over cinderblock walls.  
Rain taps the window like someone shy,  
asking to come in.

Down the hall, the communal kitchen glows—  
fluorescent, greasy, alive—  
a kettle screaming over somebody’s laughter,  
the sink full of bowls clouded with broth.  
Top Ramen blooms in chipped mugs,  
steam rising salty and gold,  
the smell of chicken powder, wet coats,  
burnt toast, detergent, nerves.

Music spills from open windows—  
bass thudding through screens,  
a guitar missing one bright string,  
someone singing off-key into the gray afternoon.  
The notes drift down into the courtyard  
where ants stitch black seams along the pavement,  
carrying crumbs like tiny students  
with impossible backpacks.

We walk to the dining hall in a loose flock,  
hoods up, shoes shining with rain,  
maple leaves plastered to the sidewalks  
like red and yellow postcards from home.  
The air tastes of coffee, cedar, and exhaust,  
and every building seems to lean closer,  
waiting to learn our names.

Inside, trays clatter, apples roll,  
voices rise warm as soup.  
We are hungry for everything—  
noodles, sleep, friendship,  
the city’s wet green breath,  
the sudden bright music  
of being unknown  
and beginning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical piece in second person about moving into an unfamiliar campus that slowly becomes home, ending with a metaphor of being released like a dove to discover yourself.
counterfactuals.output:
You arrive with your life folded into boxes,  
with hangers clinking like small uncertain bells,  
with maps you pretend to understand  
and a key that feels borrowed from someone else’s future.

At first, every hallway is a question.  
The brick buildings stare back, unnamed.  
The dining hall hums with other people’s laughter,  
and you carry your tray like a fragile offering,  
searching for a place to set down  
more than just your plate.

You learn the campus slowly—  
the library steps warmed by afternoon sun,  
the shortcut beneath the sycamores,  
the vending machine that glows at midnight  
like a tiny city that never sleeps.  
You learn which paths flood after rain,  
which benches hold the best silence,  
which windows turn gold before evening.

And somewhere between the first wrong turn  
and the hundredth walk back in the dark,  
the unfamiliar begins to loosen.  
A stranger becomes a name,  
a name becomes a knock at your door,  
a knock becomes music spilling into your room  
while you laugh on the floor  
among laundry, textbooks, and half-made plans.

You begin to belong  
not all at once,  
but in small, glowing pieces:  
your mug in the cabinet,  
your favorite tree outside class,  
your voice rising in a room  
where no one knew it before.  
The campus does not change completely—  
you do.  
You grow around its corners,  
leave traces of yourself on its sidewalks,  
and find that home can be built  
from footsteps, from friendship,  
from mornings you thought you wouldn’t survive  
and did.

Then one day,  
what once felt vast and strange  
opens its hands.  
The sky above the quad is wide,  
the wind is calling your name,  
and you understand:  
you were never only arriving.  
You were being prepared.

So you step forward,  
not as the person who first came trembling,  
but as someone remade by the journey—  
released like a dove into the bright, uncharted air,  
to discover yourself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nostalgic prose poem about living in a high-rise brick dorm, seeing red stone pathways and a 13-story tower, hearing mixed music, and feeling the salty wind while crossing Red Square.
counterfactuals.output:
I lived once in a high-rise brick dorm where the windows held the evening like small, lit aquariums, each room glowing with its own weather. From above, the red stone pathways looked almost ceremonial, threads of old clay laid carefully through the campus, leading toward the 13-story tower that stood with its familiar patience against the sky.

At night, music leaked through the walls and down the hallways—bass from one room, violin from another, someone’s bright pop chorus tangled with a song in a language I didn’t know. It all mixed together until the building itself seemed to be humming, full of restless hearts and borrowed speakers and doors left half open.

And every day, crossing Red Square, the salty wind came in from the water and touched my face like a hand from the past. It moved through my coat, lifted my hair, carried the cries of gulls and the footsteps of students hurrying somewhere important. I did not know then how much I would miss it: the brick, the tower, the red paths shining after rain, the music that never belonged to anyone alone. I was only walking across the square, young and windblown, while the whole place quietly became memory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a free verse poem about a student’s transition into university life, focusing on strange new spaces—bed, bathroom, field, classrooms—and the excitement and uncertainty of the future.
counterfactuals.output:
The bed is not mine yet,  
though my sheets have learned its corners.  
It creaks in a language  
of pipes, footsteps, doors closing  
somewhere down the hall  
after midnight.

In the bathroom,  
mirrors fog with strangers’ mornings—  
toothbrushes lined like small flags,  
shampoo bottles leaning into each other  
as if already friends.  
Water runs hot, then cold,  
then honest.  
I stand there wrapped in a towel,  
trying to remember  
the shape of home.

Outside, the field opens  
green and enormous,  
a page no one has written on.  
People cross it in every direction,  
carrying coffee, books, laughter,  
names I will learn  
or lose.  
The wind lifts the edges of my jacket  
like it is asking  
where next?

Classrooms smell of dust, markers,  
rain drying on backpacks.  
Chairs scrape their nervous music.  
A professor begins,  
and the future tilts forward—  
not a road, exactly,  
but a thousand doors  
pretending to be walls.

I am excited.  
I am uncertain.  
Both feelings live in me  
like roommates still unpacking,  
labeling boxes wrong,  
staying up too late.

At night,  
the strange bed waits.  
The bathroom hums.  
The field darkens.  
The classrooms lock their questions inside.

And I,  
half homesick, half horizon,  
step into tomorrow  
without knowing  
what to call it yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
